statements.text: Home is a small flat in Tennoji, around ten minutes on foot from the station.
I work as a nurse in the pediatric ward of Naniwa General and do three night shifts weekly.
I have a cat called Mochi, a rescue aged three, who can't stand the vacuum cleaner at all.
My morning commute to work is the Midosuji line, which is incredibly crowded, a real sardine can.
My sister Mio works baking at a little boulangerie in Kobe, and melon pan keeps arriving from her.
I started learning Korean with Duolingo for fifteen minutes a day, only because of K-dramas.
I'm still using my iPhone 12 and the battery is flat by lunch.
At the moment, Hikaru Utada is practically all I have on my playlist for the train.
My birthday present from Kenta, a surprise, was a Pixel 9, so no more worrying about the battery!
I've joined a yoga class that runs on Saturday mornings, near Shinsaibashi.
I've turned vegetarian as of the new year, and it's turned out easier in Osaka than I figured it would be.
I was transferred to the Naniwa General ICU this week and my feet are in ruins.
A tabby kitten called Kinako has joined us as Mochi's new little brother.
Shellfish allergy, as it happens: I learned it the hard way with a bowl of ramen in Hakata.
Because Kenta works as an engineer at Panasonic, he gets an odd no-overtime Wednesday each week.
This weekend Kenta and I move into a 2LDK in Fukushima ward that we signed for.
My commute to the hospital is by bike now: fifteen minutes door to door. I've stopped dreading the mornings.
These days Mio works at a specialty coffee roaster in Kyoto, having left the boulangerie.
I'm out on the Yodogawa riverside path running every Sunday, preparing for a 10k in November this year.
Duolingo is out, replaced by a weekly Korean class in Umeda; what I need is an actual human to correct me.
Every time Kenta's mum visits she brings antihistamines, since she's allergic to cats.
My Pixel is dead after I dropped it in the bath; for now I'm on a spare Galaxy A55 from Kenta.
Fish is on my plate again; going vegetarian didn't last through the night shifts, which makes me basically pescatarian at this point.
On top of that I started Spanish on Tandem; Thursdays I talk with a guy from Valencia.
The Himeji Castle 10k on November 8th: I've registered for it.
Utada's been sidelined while Fujii Kaze has moved in and taken over my playlists.
Mochi's teeth were cleaned at the vet today, and he sulked for hours.

statements.text: My 26th year in the classroom, teaching physics and maths at Tertnes high school.
I'm still behind the wheel of the 2014 Volvo V70 diesel; it has 240,000 km on the clock and just won't die.
I've been put on amlodipine by the doctor for my blood pressure: 5 mg every morning.
Our Labrador Odin is nine years old now, and he slows down on the hills.
These days Ingrid mostly works day shifts, as a nurse at Haukeland.
Four cups of black filter coffee daily, yes, I know.
In the garage I'm putting together a clinker dinghy, which has taken up my Sundays since spring.
Fana is where our house is, around twenty-five minutes south of the city centre.
As every year, it's ribbe and aquavit on Christmas Eve, and by eight I'm asleep on the sofa.
The Bybanen light rail is how I travel to school most days, and it lets me mark papers on the way.
Italian on Babbel is something I've begun, because I want to be semi-conversational before our trip to Puglia.
I've been told by the doctor to cut the coffee; two cups a day now, plus green tea in the afternoon.
The MRI says torn meniscus after my knee gave out during the hike up Ulriken.
Due in July, Sofie is expecting!
The principal at our school is Kari Sunde, who wants me to coach the physics olympiad team.
Incidentally, Odin is a yellow Lab, and his muzzle is very grey at the moment.
I finally got the arthroscopy on my knee done, and it's two weeks on crutches and I'm bored out of my mind.
An engineer's job at Equinor in Stavanger is what Mats got.
I keep reaching for a clutch that isn't there: the Model Y turned up on Friday and the V70 has gone.
Another thing I've started: restoring Ingrid's grandfather's rocking chair, and sanding it is a nightmare.
Amlodipine has been replaced by ramipril, since the swollen ankles were a pain.
I'm off until mid-August, as Friday was the last day before the summer break.
Linnea, seven pounds something, was born to Sofie on Monday, a baby girl.
The dinghy went into the water at Os this morning; I named her Snorre, and she floats!
Now I cycle to work, forty minutes each way, having got an e-bike.
Terje Moe, who started this week, is our new principal now that Kari Sunde has retired.
Ingrid has begun taking French lessons on Wednesday evenings and she's keen.
Following the blood pressure scare, I stopped coffee completely and drink only decaf and herbal tea.

statements.text: Ever since 1989 this adobe house on Candelaria has been where I live; I'm not going anywhere.
My flip phone covers all my needs. No smartphone sales pitches, please.
All day long Pepito the parakeet chirps away, which is why the radio stays on for him.
Metformin, twice daily, is what I take for my sugar, and the pharmacist fixed me up with a little weekly pill box.
I've been under Dr. Patel's care at Lovelace for eleven years; he's my doctor.
Wednesday nights are rehearsals for the choir at St. Charles, where I sing alto.
My daughter Lucia, who lives in Phoenix, is a dental hygienist, and she lectures me about flossing.
Mateo and Camila, Marcus's two kids, are making the drive down from Denver to stay for Christmas.
I'm still behind the wheel of my 2009 Buick Lucerne, which has only 61,000 miles on it.
I have cafe con leche each morning, two sugars, and don't you judge.
February 3rd is the date booked for cataract surgery on my left eye.
There's a bridge club at the community center that meets Thursday afternoons, and I've joined it.
The cataract operation was a wonderful success; the blue of the Sandias is visible to my left eye again.
Chula, a blue budgie, belonged to a neighbor who couldn't keep her, so she's mine now.
Dr. Patel retired last month, which is why I see Dr. Okafor at the UNM clinic now.
I'm learning how to FaceTime the grandkids after getting talked into an iPhone SE by Lucia.
I've planted tomatoes and green chile, so the garden is back in business.
Every Sunday I get photos from my daughter-in-law Elena, who works as a pharmacist at Kaiser.
My A1C was too high, so Dr. Okafor put Jardiance on top of the metformin: one pill each morning.
The Candelaria house is sold, and I've moved into a one-bedroom at Sandia Vista, on the east side.
I sold the Buick to the neighbor's grandson; Sandia Vista runs a shuttle, so I don't miss driving.
Rosa and I ate lunch at Garduno's yesterday; the sopapillas were huge.
The tomato days are over, and all I've got now is a pot of basil on the balcony.
I can hear the choir again, thanks to the Phonak hearing aids I got from the audiologist.
I cried more than I expected to when Pepito, aged eleven, passed away in his sleep this week.
My pressure's been creeping up, so it's decaf cafe con leche now.
I see Brenda Wells, a nurse practitioner at the Sandia Vista clinic, because Dr. Okafor left the UNM clinic.

statements.text: My job is structural engineer at Brightwater Builders, and it's mostly high-rise work around Lekki.
In Yaba we rent a three-bedroom flat; the landlord keeps on promising to fix the water pump.
A 2011 Toyota Camry, Tokunbo, is my ride; the AC is the only thing complaining.
Third Mainland Bridge is my sworn enemy; the trip to site takes around ninety minutes each way.
Ngozi, who is my wife, is a pharmacist working at a hospital in Ikeja.
We've relocated to a flat in Surulere because our landlord sold the building, and the boxes are still all over the place.
My knees hate me for it, but the banter makes five-a-side football every Saturday morning worth it.
Our compound's generator runs on petrol, and the fuel bill is killing me.
Ngozi and I will be welcoming our first baby in March!
Honestly the camera on my phone, a Tecno Camon 30, is decent.
Christmas was with my parents in Enugu, and my mum's jollof is no match for Lagos jollof, though don't tell her.
I'm giving intermittent fasting a go, with sixteen hours off and no eating after 7pm.
I've booked the PMP exam for 14 May, so every night after dinner I'm studying.
I sold the generator to my cousin, and solar panels and an inverter were put in last week.
On the 4th Chidi arrived, weighing 3.4 kg, with Ngozi's frown already.
The Tecno now lives in a drawer; Chidi's first-month photos are all on my new-to-me iPhone 14.
Monday is my start date at Arcadia Infrastructure, as a senior structural engineer, after resigning from Brightwater.
In case Arcadia ever sends me to Abidjan, I'm studying French on Busuu for twenty minutes before bed.
I got through the PMP exam!! It was four months of misery, and it paid off.
Since the new office is on Victoria Island, I now set off at 5:30am and arrive in roughly an hour.
I gave up on the fasting experiment; sleeping is worth more than an eating window when there's a newborn at home.
The client expects the Ikoyi tower package at the end of September.
My boss at Arcadia, Folake Bankole, keeps meetings short, and I love that.
In Manchester, my younger brother Obinna is a junior doctor.
That one can wait, since mid-December is the deadline for the Ajah estate package.
At last the Camry went to the scrapyard, and a dealer in Lekki sold me a 2016 Honda CR-V.
At the hospital, Ngozi reports to Dr. Adeyemi, a very serious man.
Three months in, Arcadia has just promoted me to principal structural engineer and I'm still processing it.

statements.text: My architecture degree at RMIT is in its final year, and studio is consuming my whole life.
One of my three housemates steals my yoghurt; we're in a share terrace in Brunswick East.
My weekend job is at a bike shop on Sydney Road; I mostly fix punctures and drink bad coffee.
To get to uni I catch the tram, the 96 whenever it actually shows up.
No upgrade yet, since my Pixel 7 still works even though its screen is a spiderweb.
Four years of stomach aches are explained: it turns out I'm lactose intolerant, so oat flat whites from now on.
The fan on my 2019 MacBook Pro sounds like a jet engine, and I'm still using it.
Since my October birthday I've been vegetarian, and mum is coping.
Okay Spotify, fine, I did spend nine hundred minutes listening to Phoebe Bridgers last year.
Bike-shop savings went on a splurge, a MacBook Air M3, and the jet engine has been retired.
My forearms are not impressed since I started bouldering at Northside on Tuesday nights.
Every morning before my coffee I spend ten minutes learning Japanese on WaniKani.
My brother Jonas is an electrician in the Pilbara on a FIFO roster, two weeks on then one off.
Finally some quiet: I've signed a lease on my own one-bedroom in Northcote.
The bike is my transport now: thirty minutes along the Merri Creek trail to the city.
Home from ten days in Kyoto, and my Japanese got through a ramen vending machine.
My bike is an olive-green Surly Cross-Check, should anybody ask.
Three days a week I'm interning at a small studio called Fenwick+Lowe in Collingwood, having quit the bike shop.
The topic of my thesis is adaptive reuse of old Brunswick warehouses.
My nan is horrified that I'm going vegan for June, and quite possibly forever.
Sign language has always fascinated me, so I signed up for Auslan classes on Thursday nights.
Cheese won: vegan month is over, I caved, and I'm back to vegetarian.
Three days in with the new iPhone 15 and I already miss the camera on the Pixel.
Because I'm on the iPhone now, Spotify is deleted and my playlists have moved to Apple Music.
I had to ditch the warehouses because my supervisor said so, and now the thesis is a timber community library.
The thesis is due on the 30th of October, and I've got around eleven pages.
The competition entry for Fenwick+Lowe is due on the 14th of October, which means late nights all round.

statements.text: I began this week as a pastry chef at Maison Verdier, here in Lyon. The croissants by themselves make the 4am alarm worth it.
My calves are filing a complaint: my tiny studio in Croix-Rousse, which I rent, is on the fifth floor with no elevator.
Whenever I'm home on a Sunday my six-year-old tabby Biscotte is deeply offended.
Cycling along the Rhône gets me to work in about 25 minutes, wind permitting.
I'm attempting Spanish with Duolingo, ten minutes in bed every night before I pass out.
I have a hazelnut allergy, a cruel joke for a pastry chef, and I always carry my epi pen.
A double espresso from my stovetop moka pot, no sugar, no conversation, is how every morning starts.
At a little radio station near Part-Dieu, my boyfriend Théo is a sound engineer.
The battery on my phone, a Samsung Galaxy S21, is dead by lunchtime.
I do 5k running loops in Parc de la Tête d'Or on Tuesday and Thursday evenings, every week.
For baking days I always reach for Khruangbin's Mordechai.
On my doctor's orders to cut the caffeine, mornings are genmaicha tea now.
From the shelter I adopted a second cat, Madeleine, a shy little black one.
My notice at Maison Verdier is in. Next Monday I begin as head of pastry at Café Lumière!
The camera on the iPhone 16 I unboxed today is unreal for food shots.
We finally moved, Théo and me, to a two-bedroom in Villeurbanne with an actual elevator.
Biscotte is on a diet and furious about it, because the vet says she weighs a chunky seven kilos.
Tram T1 is how I travel now, as Café Lumière is across town, and reading on my commute is finally possible.
Since May my knee has been angry, and running is banned by the doctor. Twice a week I swim at the municipal pool instead.
On top of that, I signed up for Italian classes on Tuesday evenings; why suffer in just one language?
Friday's dinner with my sister Inès was at that Lebanese place, and she cried over the baklava.
These days my baking soundtrack is Lux by Rosalía.
My mouth went itchy at brunch, so apparently I'm also mildly allergic to kiwi.
Surprise: I've gone back to coffee, though only decaf, from the old moka pot.
Now Théo is a sound designer at a video game studio in Lyon, having quit the radio.

statements.text: Monday is when the school year kicks off. After 27 years of teaching physics and maths at Älvsborgsskolan, I somehow still enjoy it.
A red villa with white corners (naturally) in Mölndal, just outside Gothenburg, is where we live.
I have no plans at all to part with my 2014 Volvo V70 diesel, which I drive and which has 240,000 km on the clock.
We have a dog named Sture, a nine-year-old golden retriever, and every walk is a polar expedition to him.
Rain or shine, Sture's three kilometres happen every morning at 6, and I got myself a headlamp for the dark months.
At my checkup my blood pressure was slightly high, which means 5 mg of amlodipine each morning for me.
The laptop I use is a ThinkPad T480, which I refuse to retire.
On Wednesday evenings there's my woodworking course, and in it I'm building a Shaker-style cabinet.
Up in Uppsala my daughter Linnea works as a vet, mostly horses and the occasional angry goat.
Constantly bragging about the fuel economy, Karin drives a white Toyota Yaris hybrid.
A second-hand Nissan Leaf replaced the old Volvo in a trade-in. The dog doesn't hear me coming, it's so quiet.
The doctor doubled my amlodipine to 10 mg because my blood pressure is still stubborn.
My woodworking course finished last night, and the finished cabinet now stands in our hallway.
Karin and I took in a one-eyed cat named Pelle; the cat adopted us, more or less.
These days mornings with Sture are a gentle one kilometre, since his hips are getting bad.
My new MacBook Air is what I'm typing this on, and the battery just won't quit.
No more teenagers hiding phones under desks: I left the classroom for good, and now I work as a lab instructor at Chalmers' physics department.
On Sunday mornings I race a Laser dinghy with the Mölndal club, now that sailing season is open.
Every Friday Karin's boss at the pharmacy, Mattias, bakes cardamom buns for the entire team.
The doctor switched me from amlodipine to losartan after my ankles swelled up like balloons.
The winter range on the Leaf was a joke, so I traded it in for a used Skoda Enyaq.
The dog crate fits in the back perfectly, and the Enyaq is the dark green 80 version.
Goosebumps all night at the Esbjörn Svensson tribute concert I went to at the Konserthuset on Friday.
Central Gothenburg is a lot louder than Mölndal ever was, I find while unpacking boxes in our new place in Linné.
On top of that, I've joined a men's choir, where I'm a second tenor and we rehearse Tuesday nights.

statements.text: My days are Figma and arguing about button radii, since I design interfaces for Finlo, a fintech startup here in Bangalore.
I have a great manager in Divya, who actually reads my design docs.
The rent is eye-watering for the three-bedroom flat in Indiranagar I share with two roommates.
My daily commute to the office is by scooter, 35 minutes when Old Airport Road behaves.
After three years, my OnePlus 9 phone is still going strong.
My whole life I've been vegetarian, because mom would disown me otherwise.
7am sharp on Saturday mornings it's badminton with the Koramangala crew.
I'm tired of smiling and nodding because my landlord only speaks Kannada, so I'm learning Kannada.
The deadline is in December for the HCI master's at TU Delft, which I'm planning to apply for.
At Infosys in Pune my brother Arjun does backend stuff that he refuses to explain.
The scooter I ride is a matte grey Honda Activa, bought second-hand from a colleague.
With Project Lotus shipping on 15 December, the whole team is sleeping under their desks.
Not until the end of January is Project Atlas due, the other thing I'm working on.
Work had a reorg. Divya moved over to the payments team, and my manager now is Karthik.
I keep all my work notes in Notion, in a color-coded system nobody else understands.
My roommate Sneha works as a corporate lawyer; her hourly billing is more than my daily earnings.
My food photos look way better than they deserve thanks to the camera on my iPhone 15.
Eggs are in now: my checkup showed low iron, and I'm no longer strictly vegetarian.
No Delft master's for me, as I decided to skip it. The money goes towards a down payment on a flat instead.
Tomorrow I begin as a senior product designer at Orchard Health, after last Friday which was my last day at Finlo.
My boss at Orchard is Meera: ex-Google, scary good at asking questions.
The scooter is collecting dust in the parking lot; with Orchard's office right by the Purple Line, I now take the metro.
I've moved into a 1BHK of my own in HSR Layout; it's my first time living alone and it's glorious.
On top of that, French on Duolingo, which I picked up purely for fun.
Saturday mornings are now bouldering at a climbing gym in HSR, instead of badminton.
My voice is completely gone after seeing Prateek Kuhad live at Palace Grounds on Friday.
Notion stays for work stuff, and I've begun using Obsidian for my personal notes.

statements.text: My job is freelance photography, mostly weddings and corporate headshots around São Paulo.
In Vila Madalena we rent a third-floor apartment, where the neighbours' samba nights make for free entertainment.
A Canon R6 is my camera body, and about 40k frames have gone through it so far.
My car is a Fiat Argo, perfect for squeezing into parking spots in São Paulo.
He's obsessed with dinosaurs, Lucas, who is eight and attends Colégio Santa Maria.
We have a dog called Pipoca, a caramel vira-lata aged three, who steals socks.
Cheap and cheerful describes my phone, a Moto G54.
After two years of jiu-jitsu on Tuesday and Thursday nights, I'm still a blue belt.
Low-carb is what I've been trying since last month, with no rice and no bread, and that's brutal in Brazil.
In Pinheiros my wife Camila runs her own clinic as a dentist.
Bia just turned five, attends a little school called Pequeno Príncipe, and comes home covered in paint every day.
My brother Thiago thinks that driving a black Jeep Renegade makes him an adventurer.
Witchcraft is the only word for the autofocus tracking on the Sony A7 IV I picked up, and the Canon has been sold.
She never lets me forget that the camera on Camila's phone, a Pixel 8, beats mine.
I'm back on rice and beans like a normal Brazilian, after low-carb lasted four months.
No more chasing invoices as a freelancer, since I joined Estúdio Lume as lead photographer.
The stabilization is absurd on my new iPhone 15 Pro, which I used to film Lucas's school recital.
A Hyundai HB20 with automatic transmission replaced the Argo in a trade, and my left leg thanks me.
At last we have a garden, having moved to a house in Granja Viana, forty minutes outside the city.
Lucas attends Escola Vila Verde now, a new school for the new house, and in week one he made a best friend named Davi.
There's a little yard at the new place, and Lucas is building a football goal there out of PVC pipes.
I quit jiu-jitsu because my shoulder said enough, and now it's futsal on Wednesday nights with the neighbourhood guys.
Bia gave the name Mel to the tiny grey cat we adopted from a rescue fair.
The film simulations are addictive on the Fujifilm X-T5 I'm shooting everything on, and the Sony has gone.
On top of that I got a DJI Mini 4 drone for aerial shots; wedding clients go nuts for them.
Eleven hours on my feet at a wedding I shot in Campos do Jordão last Saturday.

statements.text: We've been in the same two-story house in Westerville, Ohio, for 31 years, Walt and I.
A 2015 Buick Encore is what I drive; it's been a faithful little car.
I'm still on a flip phone, and I don't see why anybody would need more than that.
Wish me luck: December 8th is the date set for my knee replacement.
On my side of the bed sleeps Marmalade, my seventeen-year-old cat.
Right before bed each night, I take an atorvastatin for my cholesterol.
Fine is how the surgery went! I'm using a walker to get around the house for the time being.
Retirement is overrated, says Walt, who still works Saturdays at the hardware store.
My Phonak hearing aids are what I wear, and the left one keeps whistling at me.
At the library, on the first Thursday of each month, is when book club meets.
After thirty-eight years of nursing I still can't stay away, so Monday mornings I'm in the hospital gift shop.
I'm ahead of schedule according to the physical therapist; the walker is gone and it's just a cane now.
I'm visiting my daughter Jenny and her family, who live in Seattle, in June.
Hank, a three-year-old rescue beagle we adopted, howls at the mailman.
I'm texting the grandkids emojis nonstop now that Jenny has set me up with an iPhone SE.
On top of that, I've joined a knitting circle at church, which meets Fridays at ten.
The Buick has been swapped for a Subaru Forester; higher seats are kinder to the new knee.
My Forester is forest green, something Walt finds hilarious.
Walt keeps driving the 2008 F-150 he refuses to sell.
My doctor switched me from atorvastatin to rosuvastatin over muscle aches.
Today I walked the entire neighborhood loop without my cane, which is in the closet!
No more fumbling with tiny batteries, since I got new rechargeable Oticon hearing aids.
A one-floor ranch in Hilliard, with no stairs at all, is where we moved after selling the old house.
Marmalade slipped away last night, curled up on my side of the bed, and I'm a mess.
The library room got double-booked, so book club now meets at Jan's house on the second Tuesday evening of the month.
Monday mornings at the library I now read to kids, after quitting the hospital gift shop.
My grandson Owen named every single penguin when I took him to the zoo on Saturday.
